facts.fact_text: At the material time, the applicant was the editor-in-chief of Haykakan Zhamanak ("Armenian Times"), a daily opposition newspaper.
The applicant was an active supporter of Mr Levon Ter-Petrosyan's pre-election campaign.
The applicant was a member of Mr Levon Ter-Petrosyan's pre-election campaign.
Immediately after the announcement of the preliminary results of the 19 February 2008 presidential election, Mr Ter-Petrosyan called on his supporters to gather at Freedom Square in central Yerevan.
Mr Ter-Petrosyan called on his supporters to gather at Freedom Square in order to protest against alleged irregularities in the election process.
From 20 February 2008 onwards, nationwide daily protest rallies were held by Mr Ter-Petrosyan's supporters.
The main meeting place of Mr Ter-Petrosyan's supporters during the protest rallies from 20 February 2008 onwards was Freedom Square and the surrounding park in Yerevan.
The rallies at Freedom Square attracted at times tens of thousands of people.
Several hundred demonstrators stayed at Freedom Square and the surrounding area around the clock, having set up a camp.
The applicant alleged that he had actively participated in the demonstrations at Freedom Square, attending them on a daily basis.
The applicant alleged that he regularly gave speeches at the demonstrations at Freedom Square.
The applicant alleged that the demonstrations had been peaceful and had aimed at annulling the results of the rigged election and holding a new election.

In his appeal of 19 February 2010, the applicant argued that the speeches made at Freedom Square involved neither incitement to violence nor a violent overthrow of the government, and that Freedom Square had become an important platform for public debate on a topic of significant public concern.
In his appeal of 19 February 2010, the applicant argued that the leaders of the opposition regularly stressed in their speeches the importance of adhering to the rule of law.

The applicant alleged that the authorities had responded to the demonstrations by carrying out unlawful persecution and harassment of opposition supporters and those who had given speeches at Freedom Square.
The applicant alleged that on 23 and 24 February 2008 a number of high-ranking officials who had supported or had been suspected of supporting the opposition had been dismissed from office.
The applicant alleged that on 23 and 24 February 2008 a number of opposition leaders and activists had been arrested.
Around the same period when criminal cases were instituted against opposition leaders and activists on 1 and 2 March 2008, the applicant went into hiding.
On 4 March 2008 the applicant was formally charged under Article 225 (organising mass disorder) of the Armenian Criminal Code.
On 4 March 2008 the applicant was formally charged under Article 300 (usurpation of State power) of the Armenian Criminal Code.

The charging decision of 4 March 2008 stated that the applicant conspired with presidential candidate Levon Ter-Petrosyan and a number of his supporters to unconstitutionally usurp State power by destabilising the internal political situation in Armenia if Levon Ter-Petrosyan were to suffer a defeat at the presidential election.

The charging decision of 4 March 2008 stated that the applicant, together with Levon Ter-Petrosyan and a number of his supporters, starting from the day after the 19 February 2008 election, organised and held in Yerevan continuous mass public events, marches and round-the-clock demonstrations and sit-ins in violation of the procedure prescribed by law.

The charging decision of 4 March 2008 stated that the applicant publicly gave incendiary speeches and made public calls inciting to civil disobedience, disobedience against lawful orders of the law-enforcement authorities and assistance in disintegration of the State system and overthrow of the current government.

The charging decision of 4 March 2008 stated that on 1 March 2008, addressing the crowd gathered at the area adjacent to the Yerevan Mayor's Office as an official election assistant of Levon Ter-Petrosyan, the applicant instigated and organised mass disorder which involved mass violence, widespread massacre, arson, destruction and damage of public and private property, overt looting, armed resistance against public officials, mass assaults on public officials with the use of firearms and explosives, and murders.
On 1 July 2009 the applicant voluntarily turned himself in to the authorities.
On 3 July 2009 the applicant was brought before the Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court of Yerevan.
On 3 July 2009 the Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court of Yerevan decided to detain the applicant for a period of two months.
On 16 July 2009 the Criminal Court of Appeal upheld the decision to detain the applicant.
On 27 August 2009 the Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court of Yerevan extended the applicant's detention by two months on the same grounds as the initial detention order.
On 12 October 2009, following the completion of the investigation, the Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court of Yerevan took a decision setting the case down for trial.

In its 12 October 2009 decision, the Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court of Yerevan ruled that the applicant's detention should remain unchanged, reasoning that the applicant had been accused of, among others, a serious crime for which a penalty of from four to ten years' imprisonment is prescribed.
On 19 January 2010 the Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court of Yerevan found the applicant guilty under Article 225 § 1 of the Armenian Criminal Code (organising mass disorder).
On 19 January 2010 the Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court of Yerevan sentenced the applicant to seven years' imprisonment.
On 19 February 2010 the applicant lodged an appeal against his conviction.
In his appeal of 19 February 2010, the applicant argued that his conviction had violated the guarantees of Article 10 of the Convention.
In his appeal of 19 February 2010, the applicant argued that his conviction had violated the guarantees of Article 11 of the Convention.
On 9 March 2010 the Criminal Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant's appeal and upheld his conviction.
On 10 April 2010 the applicant lodged an appeal on points of law.
On 30 April 2010 the Court of Cassation of Armenia declared the applicant's appeal on points of law inadmissible for lack of merit.

On 24 March 2009 the charge against the applicant under Article 300 of the Armenian Criminal Code (usurpation of State power) was dropped.
The charge under Article 300 of the Armenian Criminal Code was dropped because that provision had been amended and as a result was no longer applicable.
On 19 January 2010 the Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court of Yerevan found the applicant guilty under Article 225 § 1 of the Armenian Criminal Code (organising mass disorder).
The Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court of Yerevan concluded that the events in question amounted to 'mass disorder' within the meaning of Article 225 § 1 of the Armenian Criminal Code.
The Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court of Yerevan concluded that the applicant's actions fell within the scope of Article 225 § 1 of the Armenian Criminal Code.

The Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court of Yerevan found it established that Serzh Sargsyan won the presidential election held on 19 February 2008.

The Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court of Yerevan found it established that the applicant, together with A.A., S.S., H.H., M.M. and S.M. (who had already been convicted under Article 225 § 1 of the Armenian Criminal Code in a separate set of proceedings) and a number of other persons, starting from 20 February 2008, carried out organisational activities for the purpose of creating discontent in society towards the conduct and results of the election and preparing the crowd gathered at Freedom Square for use of violence and disobedience.

The Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court of Yerevan found it established that rods, clubs, armature, petrol bombs, metal constructions used as missile weapons, firearms and ammunition were distributed to a group of participants of the assembly at Freedom Square.

The Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court of Yerevan found it established that with the intention of inciting and carrying out mass disorder in Yerevan on 1 March 2008, the members of the group formed groups of people ready to use violence on a mass scale and organised distribution among those persons of illegally obtained firearms, ammunition, explosive substances, explosive devices, bladed weapons and various objects adapted to inflict violence.

The Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court of Yerevan held that, having found out about the imminent arrival of the police forces in the early morning of 1 March 2008, the applicant, together with his co-thinkers, woke up those camping at Freedom Square and called on them to arm themselves and to give a 'proper welcome' to the police.

The Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court of Yerevan held that as a result of the applicant's actions, the crowd attacked the police officers who had approached and asked to carry out an inspection for weapons.

The Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court of Yerevan held that the police operation at Freedom Square eventually led to the discovery of various weapons and ammunition, which had been brought to Freedom Square to be used during the planned mass disorder.

The Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court of Yerevan found that the participants of the assembly, led by the applicant, A.A. and others, moved to and gathered in the area adjacent to the Myasnikyan monument, an important intersection of several streets in Yerevan situated in the vicinity of the French, Italian and Russian embassies.

The Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court of Yerevan found that at around 11 a.m. on 1 March 2008 the participants of the mass disorder blocked Grigor Lusavorich Street by placing trolleybuses across the driveway, after which they attacked the police officers who were preserving public order.

The Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court of Yerevan found that the applicant, together with A.A., S.M. and others, rejected the offer made by the authorities to move the assembly to another location for the purpose of preserving public order and ensuring the safety of participants.

The Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court of Yerevan found that the applicant, with his speeches and orders, organised and oversaw keeping the gathered crowd in the same location for as long as possible and derailing its relocation, as well as the process of arming themselves with objects adapted to inflict injuries and other objects at hand, assaulting the police officers and showing active disobedience to their lawful orders.

The Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court of Yerevan found that, as organised and directly instructed by the applicant, S.S. and others, barricades were created by damaging transportation means and other property and by putting them out of order.

The Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court of Yerevan found that the applicant gave instructions to the demonstrators to arm themselves and to be ready to resist, as well as to recruit new people at any cost.

The Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court of Yerevan found that the applicant continuously circulated among the participants in the mass disorder and organised the formation and dislocation of their groups.

The Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court of Yerevan found that the applicant gave concrete instructions to participants to split into groups, build barricades, arm themselves with stones, sticks and other objects in order to injure the police officers, and grab batons and shields from the police officers.
The Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court of Yerevan found that the applicant publicly encouraged the participants in the mass disorder to grab shields and batons from the police officers.

The Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court of Yerevan found that the applicant called on soldiers and police officers involved in maintaining public order not to carry out their duties, to join the participants in the mass disorder and to turn their weapons towards the authorities.
The Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court of Yerevan found that the applicant gave concrete instructions on how to reinforce positions and to prepare for new acts of violence.

The Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court of Yerevan found that the applicant made public declarations about areas captured by the participants in the disorder and declared that all the soldiers had fled and the entire process was under their control, in order to keep the participants in the mass disorder around and to inspire them.

The Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court of Yerevan found that the applicant regularly invited other organisers of the mass disorder for consultations in order to organise and coordinate the activities of its participants.

The Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court of Yerevan found that the applicant regularly exchanged information with A.A. and S.S. about the massacre, arson, intentional destruction, damage and looting of property taking place on Grigor Lusavorich, Mashtots, Leo and Paronyan streets of Yerevan.
The Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court of Yerevan concluded that the events in question amounted to 'mass disorder' within the meaning of Article 225 § 1 of the Armenian Criminal Code.

The Criminal Court of Appeal held in its 9 March 2010 decision that during the demonstrations held in various parts of Yerevan the applicant had committed a criminal offence, namely organising mass disorder.

The Criminal Court of Appeal held in its 9 March 2010 decision that, taking into account the weapons and ammunition found at Freedom Square, the assembly at Freedom Square had not been peaceful, and nor had the assembly in the area adjacent to the Yerevan Mayor's Office.

The applicant alleged that the police had attacked and brutally beaten the demonstrators camping at Freedom Square in the early morning of 1 March 2008.

The applicant alleged that after the demonstrators had fled to the area of the French Embassy and had been joined by thousands of others, the police and military forces and equipment had started to encircle that area.
The applicant alleged that another brutal attack had been launched on the demonstrators near the French Embassy area, and the demonstrators had had to defend themselves with random objects.
The applicant alleged that the demonstrators had barricaded the area near the French Embassy with public and private vehicles and continued the demonstration peacefully.

The applicant alleged that he, together with a number of other opposition leaders, had called on the public to stay calm and tried to prevent new clashes by creating a human chain between the police forces and the demonstrators.
The applicant alleged that the demonstrators had been waiting for Mr Ter-Petrosyan's arrival but Mr Ter-Petrosyan had been placed under house arrest in the meantime.

The applicant alleged that several more attacks had been launched on the demonstrators, using not only crowd control weapons but also live ammunition, snipers and military equipment, resulting in up to ten deaths and numerous injured.

In his appeal of 19 February 2010, the applicant alleged that the authorities had embarked on a campaign of political repression against the supporters of Mr Ter-Petrosyan before and during the peaceful demonstrations held at Freedom Square.

In his appeal of 19 February 2010, the applicant alleged that the authorities had initiated unlawful criminal prosecution of supporters of Mr Ter-Petrosyan following the dispersal of the assembly on 1 March 2008.

In his appeal of 19 February 2010, the applicant argued that the speeches made at Freedom Square involved neither incitement to violence nor a violent overthrow of the government, and that Freedom Square had become an important platform for public debate on a topic of significant public concern.
In his appeal of 19 February 2010, the applicant argued that the leaders of the opposition regularly stressed in their speeches the importance of adhering to the rule of law.

In his appeal of 19 February 2010, the applicant denied that he had guided the demonstrators to the area of the Yerevan Mayor's Office and the Myasnikyan monument, submitting that the demonstrators had fled to that area on escaping from the police and being pursued by them after their brutal dispersal from Freedom Square.

In his appeal of 19 February 2010, the applicant contested that the actions of the demonstrators could be characterised as 'mass disorder' and argued that, even assuming they could, the Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court of Yerevan had failed to indicate any concrete actions taken by him towards the organisation of such mass disorder.

In his appeal of 19 February 2010, the applicant argued that there had been no preliminary agreement between the so-called organisers of the alleged mass disorder and that some of them had not even been familiar with each other before meeting for the first time in court.
In his appeal of 19 February 2010, the applicant argued that he had never incited to violence or any other actions which could be characterised as 'mass disorder'.

In his appeal of 19 February 2010, the applicant argued that when he arrived at the vicinity of the Yerevan Mayor's Office, the demonstrators had already barricaded themselves and detached various objects from a nearby construction site for self-defence.

The Criminal Court of Appeal held in its 9 March 2010 decision that the applicant had participated in the assembly held from 20 February to 1 March 2008, during which he had availed himself of his freedom of expression by freely imparting information and ideas without any interference by the authorities.

The Criminal Court of Appeal held in its 9 March 2010 decision that during the demonstrations held in various parts of Yerevan the applicant had committed a criminal offence, namely organising mass disorder.

The Criminal Court of Appeal held in its 9 March 2010 decision that the applicant had been prosecuted for criminal conduct during the demonstrations, rather than for his participation in the demonstrations and expressing his opinion, and therefore there had not been an interference with the applicant's right to freedom of peaceful assembly under Article 11 of the Convention.

The Criminal Court of Appeal held in its 9 March 2010 decision that, taking into account the weapons and ammunition found at Freedom Square, the assembly at Freedom Square had not been peaceful, and nor had the assembly in the area adjacent to the Yerevan Mayor's Office.

In its Resolutions regarding the 19 February 2008 presidential election and the events that followed, the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe condemned the arrest and continuing detention of scores of persons, including more than 100 opposition supporters and three members of parliament.

The Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe condemned the arrest and continuing detention of opposition supporters and members of parliament on seemingly artificial and politically motivated charges, especially those under Articles 225 and 300 of the Armenian Criminal Code.

Relevant extracts of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe Resolutions and a number of other relevant international materials regarding the 19 February 2008 presidential election and post-election events can be found in Mushegh Saghatelyan v. Armenia (no. 23086/08, §§ 125-34, 20 September 2018) and Myasnik Malkhasyan v. Armenia (no. 49020/08, §§ 50-57, 15 October 2020).
